questions.q: What did the 1990 study of 257 musicians find?
a: Top performers showed no early talent and improved at the same rate
Top performers showed obvious gifts from their first lessons
Top performers practiced far less than their peers
Top performers started playing at a much later age
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the best musicians had no head start and needed just as much practice as everyone else.

questions.q: What distinction does Colvin draw in lesson 1?
a: Practice is not the same thing as experience
Talent matters more than effort in the long run
Experience always produces steady improvement
Practice only works for young children
questions.why: Lesson 1 says repeating the same job builds the same experience rather than new skill.

questions.q: How much older are Nobel winners today than a century ago when they make their breakthrough?
a: About six years older
About two years older
About ten years older
About the same age
questions.why: Lesson 2 uses the six-year shift to show that mastering a field now takes longer than it used to.

questions.q: Which advantage does a child have when starting deliberate practice?
a: Fewer adult responsibilities and more time to practice
A stronger tolerance for failure and criticism
Better access to expert coaching
More money to spend on lessons
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists time, a family support network and a young, fast-learning brain.

questions.q: What is the multiplier effect in lesson 3?
a: A slight early edge brings more motivation, coaching and support
Doubling your practice time doubles your skill
Talent grows automatically as a person gets older
Competition pushes peers to improve together
questions.why: Lesson 3 says being a little better than peers triggers outside support that compounds the advantage.
